summary: AEGIS-0G is an interactive Mission Control dashboard and 3D progressive fire-damage simulator that uses AI synthesis to transform decades of NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion research into actionable fire-safety guidance for spacecraft, lunar bases, and Martian rovers.
details:
The Problem:

Future lunar bases, surface rovers, and deep-space habitats will operate in high-oxygen (30% O2 or higher) and reduced-pressure (10.2 psi or lower) atmospheres where microgravity and partial-gravity fires behave unpredictably—forming invisible cool flames, coagulated smoke aerosols, and accelerated flame spread. However, critical findings across NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion database remain dispersed across dense technical reports and datasets.

Our Solution (AEGIS-0G):

We built a zero-latency, interactive web platform combining two mission-critical engineering modules focused strictly on habitable cabin fire safety (excluding rocket propellants):

1. NASA PSI Combustion Explorer and Comparison Matrix:

Synthesizes and compares real NASA low-gravity fire investigations across Prevention (SAFFIRE-I, SAFFIRE-II, SAFFIRE-III, BASS, BASS-II), Detection (SAME, DAFT), and Suppression (FLEX, ACME). Researchers, engineers, and students can filter investigations by mission environment, compare fuel samples, oxygen concentrations, cabin pressures, airflow velocities, and sensor suites side-by-side, and review terrestrial Earth spin-offs such as fine-water-mist extinguishers and multi-wavelength smoke detectors.

2. Interactive 3D Habitat and Progressive Fire-Damage Lab:

A WebGL/Three.js virtual testbed modeling Orbital Spacecraft (0g), Lunar Bases (0.16g), and Martian Pressurized Rovers (0.38g). Users adjust cabin oxygen, air pressure, and ventilation velocity with real-time Green/Yellow/Red hazard indicators, ignite spacecraft materials, and fast-forward past T + 2:00 minutes to observe progressive structural charring, smoke accumulation, and suppression response.
